blocks.label: Times of day
blocks.rationale: The parts of the day that routines and plans hang on, plus kesa and konban for this morning and tonight.
blocks.interference: kesa and konban always mean this morning and tonight. Bare asa and yoru just name the part of the day, and context picks which day: yoru denwa suru ne said at lunch means tonight, and asa denwa suru ne said at night means tomorrow morning. konban wa hima? starts exactly like the greeting konbanwa. If more words follow, it means tonight.

items.use: The morning as a part of the day, for routines (asa hayaku, asagohan) and spans like asa kara (since the morning).

example.english: I'll call you in the morning.

examplePolite.english: I'll call you in the morning.

items.notes: For 'this morning' say kesa or kyou no asa.

items.use: Midday and the daytime as opposed to yoru, mostly in set phrases: hiru made (till noon), hiru kara (from noon), hirusugi (just after noon), hirugohan (lunch). Casually, bare hiru also means lunch (hiru nani taberu?).
items.notes: For 'at lunchtime' say ohiru ni (ohiru ni denwa suru ne). ohiru on its own also means lunch, and hiruma means the daytime hours. For the afternoon say gogo (午後, #1394): gogo wa hima?

items.use: Evening and night, for plans and routines. kyou no yoru is a common casual way to say tonight.
items.notes: ban (晩, #4729) is a near-synonym that lives in set words: konban, konbanwa, bangohan (dinner), maiban (every night). For late afternoon to dusk say yuugata (夕方, #2124); yoru starts once it is dark.

items.use: One word for kyou no asa. It often looks back at earlier this morning with past tense (kesa nani tabeta?), but while it is still morning non-past is fine too: kesa wa samui ne.

example.english: It was cold this morning, huh.

examplePolite.ja: 今朝は寒かったですね。
examplePolite.english: It was cold this morning, wasn't it?

items.notes: An irregular word (not kon-asa). Like kyou, it takes no ni. kyou no asa means the same and is always safe.

items.use: Tonight, for evening plans and invitations. It has the same kon- ('this') as konshuu and kongetsu.

example.english: Want to go for a drink tonight?

examplePolite.ja: 今晩飲みに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go for a drink tonight?

items.freqNote: 今晩(こんばん) #3984; same-meaning 今夜(こんや) #770
items.notes: konya (今夜) means the same and is more frequent in dramas, so recognise it. Among friends, plain kyou often covers tonight: kyou nomi ni ikanai? For last night say yuube (ゆうべ, #2525) or kinou no yoru.

blocks.label: Last, this, next week
blocks.rationale: kinou, kyou and ashita stretched to weeks: sen- is last, kon- is this, rai- is next. Plus the weekend that everyone asks about.
blocks.interference: senshuu, konshuu and raishuu differ only in the first syllable. sen- goes with past tense like kinou, and rai- with plans like ashita. Like kinou and ashita, all three take no ni: raishuu iku, not raishuu ni iku. shuumatsu is the weekend, and the tense tells you which one; it can take ni or go without.

items.use: Last week, for recaps. Like kinou, it pairs with past tense, and the same sen- gives sengetsu.

examplePolite.ja: 先週は忙しかったです。

items.use: This week. It works like kyou, taking past or non-past tense, and the same kon- gives kongetsu and konban.

example.romaji: konshuu wa chotto isogashii n da.
example.ja: 今週はちょっと忙しいんだ。
example.english: I'm kind of busy this week.

examplePolite.romaji: konshuu wa chotto isogashii n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今週はちょっと忙しいんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm a bit busy this week.

items.use: Next week, a scheduling staple. Like ashita, it pairs with non-past tense, and the same rai- gives raigetsu and rainen.

The weekend, mostly in small-talk questions. Non-past (nani suru?) asks about the coming weekend, past (nani shita?) about the one just gone, and -teru about habit: shuumatsu wa nani shiteru no? (what do you usually do at weekends?).

example.english: What are you doing this weekend?

examplePolite.english: What are you doing this weekend?

items.notes: To pin down which weekend, say konshuumatsu (今週末) or raishuumatsu (来週末), one word each. konshuu no shuumatsu also works.

blocks.label: Last, this, next month
blocks.rationale: The sen-, kon- and rai- of the week words applied to months, with no exceptions.
blocks.interference: sengetsu, kongetsu and raigetsu differ only in the first syllable, exactly like senshuu, konshuu and raishuu. Like the week words, they take no ni: raigetsu hikkosu, not raigetsu ni hikkosu.

items.use: Last month, for recaps. It uses the same sen- as senshuu, so it pairs with past tense.

examplePolite.ja: 先月引っ越したんです。

items.use: This month, for budgets, schedules and deadlines. It uses the same kon- as konshuu.
Next month, for plans and deadlines. It uses the same rai- as raishuu.

blocks.label: Last, this, next year
blocks.rationale: The same grid for years, where two of the three words are irregular.
blocks.interference: Only rainen fits the sen-/kon-/rai- pattern: this year is kotoshi and last year is kyonen. kyonen has a short kyo- (kyo-ne-n), unlike the long kyou of 'today', so don't stretch it. Like the week and month words, all three take no ni.

items.use: Last year, the usual anchor for recaps. Like kinou, it pairs with past tense.
items.notes: It breaks the sen- pattern. Say a short kyo- (kyo-ne-n, three beats), not the long kyou of 'today'. sakunen (昨年, #5231) is the formal version heard in business talk and the news: recognise it, but say kyonen even in desu/masu.

items.use: This year, for yearly plans and recaps, and the New Year line kotoshi mo yoroshiku.
items.notes: It breaks the kon- pattern: kotoshi. The kon- reading turns up in work talk as konnendo (今年度, this fiscal year).

items.use: Next year, for plans and hopes. It is the one year word that fits the rai- pattern of raishuu and raigetsu.

blocks.label: So far, from now
blocks.rationale: Phrases that place a statement relative to now: up to now, from here on, as things stand, and for a while.
blocks.interference: ima made and ima no tokoro can both mean 'so far'. ima made looks back, and ima made wa with past tense hints that something has changed, while ima no tokoro reports a state that still holds. kore kara looks forward.

items.use: Looks back over the time up to now, often with past tense or experience (ima made ichido mo nai), and in ima made nani shiteta no? (what have you been doing all this time?). kore made is a more formal synonym.

example.romaji: ima made wa daijoubu datta n da kedo.
example.ja: 今までは大丈夫だったんだけど。
example.english: It was fine until now, though.

examplePolite.romaji: ima made wa daijoubu datta n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 今までは大丈夫だったんですけど。
examplePolite.english: It was fine until now, though.

items.freqNote: 今まで(いままで) #370; formal-leaning これまで #952
items.notes: ima made arigatou is the standard thanks when someone leaves or something ends.

items.use: Points forward from this moment, to something about to start (kore kara dekakeru) or to everything from here on. ima kara means the same for the immediate moment.

examplePolite.ja: これからどうしますか？

items.freqNote: これから #2065 (likely undercounted: the tokenizer can split これ + から); near-synonym 今から(いまから) #972
items.notes: kore kara mo yoroshiku ('I'm counting on you going forward') is a common closing line.

items.use: Hedges a status or plan as true for now but open to change (ima no tokoro yotei nai).

examplePolite.ja: 今のところ大丈夫です。

items.freqNote: 今のところ(いまのところ) #2474
items.notes: toriaezu is 'for now' for a stopgap action, while ima no tokoro describes how things stand.

items.use: Gives a vague stretch of time, short or long, without numbers (shibaraku matte, shibaraku aenai).

example.english: I'll be busy for a while.

examplePolite.ja: しばらく忙しいんです。
examplePolite.english: I'll be busy for a while.

items.notes: For 'long time no see', friends say hisashiburi and the polite form is ohisashiburi desu (お久しぶり, #1495). shibaraku desu is an older, formal version: recognise it, but don't produce it.

changelog.change: Times of day interference rewritten (natural + nuance, major). kesa/konban are pinned to today; bare asa/yoru take their day from context; the greeting trap is now konban wa hima?, which sounds exactly like konbanwa. use: asa gohan -> asagohan, matching the joined compound spelling used elsewhere in the list.

BLOCK PLACEMENT, NOT APPLIED HERE (nuance, major): only the additions are returned, so the merge must do this. Insert the four time-noun blocks (Times of day; Last, this, next week; Last, this, next month; Last, this, next year) directly after A1 'Now and nearby days', before 'Already, still, finally'. Keep 'So far, from now' last, after 'Until, by, while still'.

The form review's request to re-gloss the example as 'in the evening' was not applied: natural and nuance both confirm 'tonight' is correct, and the contradiction is fixed in the interference instead.

reviewSummaries: natural: All 19 additions belong and most examples sound native (kesa, the week, month and year sentences, konban, shuumatsu, ima no tokoro, kore kara). Four need real fixes: the hiru example (bare 昼 used as a time adverb sounds off), the ima-made example (cut off without けど), the Times-of-day interference line, which contradicts the block's own 'tonight' translation, and the shibaraku note presenting the dated shibaraku desu as the polite 'long time no see' (ohisashiburi desu). The rest is polish on notes and English. I checked every alsoIn pointer and frequency rank with the tool.

nuance: All 19 items earn a place and nothing needs cutting. Every freqRank matches the tool output, and the alsoIn pointers check out. Main problems: kesa's 'morning is over' reason is wrong; the Times of day interference contradicts its own 'tonight' example; the no-ni trap (*raishuu ni) is missing; and shibaraku's note mislabels shibaraku desu as the polite pair of hisashiburi (it should be ohisashiburi desu).
Structure: the three plain time-noun blocks should go right after A1, not after the clause-timing patterns, and the 6-item Months and years block should be split. The rest is polish: ban/bangohan, yuube, a gogo gap, the lunch gloss for hiru, and gloss consistency.

form: The mechanical checks pass. All 19 romaji/kana/ja triples follow the convention, the examples match word for word, the polite pairs are correct, there are no duplicate slugs, the blocks hold 5/4/6/4 items, all 25 checked freqRanks match the tool exactly, all 16 checked alsoIn pointers are valid (10-list-nouns #96–99, utility-vocab times-of-day and relative-periods), and every prereq slug exists (ima, made, kore). Two content errors are worth fixing before merge. The yoru example renders bare yoru as 'tonight', which contradicts the block's own interference note. 'kyonen starts like kyou' misstates vowel length for an audio-first learner. The rest is polish: a kon'ya apostrophe, mismatched kore-kara English, kotoshi/shibaraku notes, missing particle pointers and an likely-undercounted これから note.

blocks.label: More enders
blocks.rationale: Three endings built on items you already have: -te plus ne for a friendly ask, n da plus yo for an insistent reason, and darou, the plain form of deshou, for wondering aloud.
blocks.interference: darou is the plain deshou, but in casual speech only its wondering uses (nan darou, daijoubu darou ka) are neutral, so say kamo for 'probably' and desho? for 'right?'. n da yo pushes a reason across where n da just explains, and -te ne assumes a yes where -te kurenai? asks.

items.use: Adds ne to a casual -te request so it sounds warm rather than bossy. It is the everyday way to ask or remind friends, family and kids (mata renraku shite ne, ki o tsukete ne). It assumes they'll go along, so it's a friendly instruction, not a question.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと待ってね
example.english: Sorry, hang on a sec, OK?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと待ってくださいね

items.freqNote: no usable rank — てね #24031 undercounts (tokenizer splits)
items.notes: -naide ne is the 'don't' version (wasurenaide ne). -te kudasai ne sounds like giving instructions, which is fine from staff or between coworkers but bossy to a superior, so ask them with -te moraemasu ka. Mid-story -te ne (kinou eki ni itte ne, ...) is just 'and then' plus ne, not a request.

items.use: Gives the listener an explanation they don't have yet, with yo pushing it across: why something happened, news, or a correction. Everyone uses it. After a question word it turns into a rough, masculine rebuke (nani shiteru n da yo! = what the hell are you doing?), so recognise that one; the neutral version is nani shiteru no!?

example.english: I've got a headache, that's why.

examplePolite.romaji: atama ga itai n desu yo
examplePolite.english: I have a headache, you see.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; rank of んだ (んだよ not found)
items.notes: no yo (atama itai no yo) is the feminine version, now mostly heard from older women and in dramas; young women just say n da yo or no. Giving a superior an excuse with n desu yo sounds defensive; plain n desu is safer.

items.use: The plain form of deshou. Wondering aloud is neutral and everyone says it, whether with a question word (nan darou, dou darou, doko itta n darou) or with ka (daijoubu darou ka). As a falling 'probably' (ashita wa ame darou) or the rising tag daro? (right?), it sounds masculine and blunt, so most casual speakers say kamo (or tabun) for 'probably' and desho? for 'right?' instead.

examplePolite.ja: 会議はいつでしょうか
examplePolite.english: When is the meeting, I wonder?

items.freqNote: #102 だろう (だろ #119; でしょう #147, which also counts casual でしょ)
items.notes: dou darou on its own is a handy non-answer ('hmm, hard to say'). Polite deshou is neutral for everyone, whether as 'probably' (ame deshou) or as deshou ka (I wonder). In fast speech the wondering form is often just daro, said falling (itsu daro); that is neutral. Only the rising daro? (right?) is the masculine tag.

blocks.label: Speaker-marking enders
blocks.rationale: Variants of yo and ne that you'll hear constantly from friends and in dramas, each marking the speaker as young, male, rough, feminine or from Kansai. Mid-sentence sa is fine in moderation and yo na is normal if you're a man; zo and the rising wa are mostly for recognising, not copying.
blocks.interference: zo and wa both take the place of yo: zo pushes, falling wa just announces your own move or reaction, and rising wa is the feminine one. sa fills pauses inside a sentence the way mid-sentence ne does, and yo na is simply a masculine yo ne.

items.use: Dropped after a phrase to hold the listener's attention while you talk (ano sa = hey, listen; kinou sa, ...). Both genders use it, younger speakers especially. At the end of a sentence it sounds offhand and leans masculine (nantoka naru sa = eh, it'll work out).

example.romaji: kinou sa, tanaka-san ni atta n da
example.ja: 昨日さ、田中さんに会ったんだ
example.english: So yesterday, I ran into Tanaka-san.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou desu ne, tanaka-san ni atta n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 昨日ですね、田中さんに会ったんですよ
examplePolite.english: So yesterday, I ran into Tanaka-san.

items.freqNote: #88 さ, which may also count the noun suffix -sa split off words like 優しさ/大切さ (not found whole), so treat as an upper bound; さあ 'well' #263 is separate
items.notes: It replaces da, never follows it (sou sa, not *sou da sa). Tacked onto every phrase it sounds sloppy; mid-sentence ne does the same job more softly.

items.use: The masculine counterpart of yo ne. It checks or agrees with something you both believe (sou da yo na = yeah, exactly). Men say it all the time with friends; women mostly say yo ne.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa yasumi desu yo ne?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — よな #12379 undercounts (tokenizer splits)
items.notes: Said to yourself, it's a rueful 'yeah, I guess' (muri da yo na...). Polite speech has only desu yo ne, so the gender difference disappears.

items.english: I'll..., then (falling, announcing) / soft assertion (rising, fem)
items.use: Two endings that sound alike. Said falling, it announces your own decision or reaction (jaa, iku wa; muri da wa); it is Kansai, gender-neutral and now common among young people everywhere. Said rising, it is the soft feminine assertion of older women and drama characters, dated in real Tokyo speech.
items.freqNote: #75 わ, which merges rising (feminine) and falling (Kansai / neutral) wa (わよ #489, わね #647)
items.notes: Polite speech drops it (jaa, ikimasu ne; muri desu ne), though Kansai speakers keep it (ikimasu wa). It is unrelated to the topic particle wa (kore wa). Record and drill only the falling wa; the rising one is the feminine wa.

items.use: A forceful masculine yo for warnings, rallying a group and announcements (abunai zo!, iku zo!). You hear it constantly from fathers, coaches, bosses and drama heroes; recognise it, but say yo.
items.notes: Pepping yourself up (yoshi, ganbaru zo) is the mildest use, and women say that too. ze (ikou ze, yatta ze) is its swaggering cousin, always aimed at a buddy and never said to yourself; most men only say it jokingly.

Kept as a 3-item block. Place it after F5 in course order so that n-da, kana, te-request and desho all come before it. Interference now names the neutral darou ka use and pairs kamo with 'probably' and desho? with 'right?'.

New rationale says mid-sentence sa is fine in moderation, yo na is normal for men, and zo and rising wa are mostly for recognising (natural + nuance). Removed ze from the interference line.

Notes: -te kudasai ne is an instructing tone (fine from staff or between coworkers, bossy to a superior), and added the audio trap of mid-story -te ne (kinou eki ni itte ne, ...). alsoIn: added 13-list-exit-battery #62.

Notes: no yo is now plainly feminine and mostly heard from older women and in dramas (merged natural + nuance wording). Added that n desu yo as an excuse to a superior sounds defensive. Dropped the na n da yo line, which F2 already covers.

examplePolite added: jaa, ikimasu yo (all three reviewers). contrastGroup zo-ze-wa -> zo-wa. Notes now cover ze as a recognition pointer: swaggering cousin, aimed at a buddy, mostly said jokingly.

reviewSummaries: natural: All eight casual examples are things people really say, and the jaa, iku wa / zo / ze set is a good audio contrast. The one serious problem is wa-ending: its English gloss describes the feminine/Kansai use, but the example and the recommended use are the neutral falling wa. Smaller fixes: fill the missing polite examples (wa, zo), tighten the darou, sa and no yo notes, and soften the "don't copy" wording of the Mostly heard block. ze should be folded into zo's notes rather than kept as its own card. Frequency ranks match the tool output (てね #24031, んだ #20, だろう #102, さ #88, よな #12379, わ #75, ぞ #82, ぜ #614), and the alsoIn pointers check out.

nuance: All 8 freqRanks match the tool output, and the alsoIn pointers check out. Overall: dissolve the 3-item 'More enders' grab-bag into F2/F3/F4 (each then has 5 items), and cut ze. Item fixes:
- darou: give it a kana-kke contrastGroup and a base sentence that matches the group.
- n da yo: warn that the question-word rebuke (nani shiteru n da yo!) is rough and masculine.
- wa: rewrite the gloss around the falling 'announcing' wa, add the 'dated' flag, and set polite to null.
- zo: add a polite example.
- Notes on te-ne, yo-na and n-da-yo, plus the 'Mostly heard' label, need polishing.

form: The form is clean overall. All 13 example romaji/ja pairs match word for word and the kana and polite pairs agree. All 13 cited ranks match the frequency tool (plus 12 more spot checks). All 5 alsoIn pointers are real (12-te #3, 13-battery #93, kotoba ne/yo). All prereqs name real F slugs, there are no duplicate slugs, and the blocks have 3 and 5 items.
The one real risk: wa-ending's example must be recorded falling, and nothing in the data says so. The other fixes are smaller. wa, zo and ze have polite values but no polite example (the only such items in the list), and ze's polite field should also cover desu yo. Then there are freqNote fixes (さ may count the noun suffix -sa; でしょう #147 also counts でしょ), darou's missing contrastGroup and its 'probably'/'right?' wording, and one missed pointer.
